articles.title: EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: EPHEMERIS Vol. 2 No. 5 is the official publication of the San Jose Astronomical Association for May 1990. This document likely served as a newsletter or bulletin providing information to its members during that specific month.

articles.title: FIELD OF VIEW YOSEMITE STAR PARTY
articles.summary: This article announces the upcoming annual SJAA/Yosemite Star Party on July 20th & 21st at Glacier Point, emphasizing its moonless dark skies, though the reservation list is full. It also details the 10th Annual Astronomical Auction on May 5th, including a flea market, to replace the month's general meeting. Additionally, it provides an observing report on Comet Austin, noting its disappointing brightness, and mentions an ongoing observational astronomy class.

articles.title: BRANHAM LANE STAR PARTIES - WE WANT YOU!
articles.summary: This article announces a packed schedule of events for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) for May and June. Highlights include multiple public star parties at various parks, the 10th Annual Astronomical Auction, board meetings, and introductory astronomy classes. A general meeting featuring a talk on meteors and near-Earth asteroids is also planned.

articles.title: MAY STARRY NIGHTS
articles.summary: This article announces a series of 'Starry Nights' public observing events scheduled on select dates from July through December, including July 27, August 31, September 28, October 26, and December 28. Attendees are encouraged to bring their telescopes and invite friends. For additional information, Tom Ahl or Jim Van Nuland can be contacted.

articles.title: ONE OF THIS MONTH'S FINEST
articles.summary: The article highlights NGC 3242, "The Ghost of Jupiter," as a recommended planetary nebula for observation this month due to its magnitude and size. It also details the San Jose Astronomical Association's 1990 Messier Marathon, which was held under thin, cloudy conditions, limiting participants' ability to complete the marathon but still allowing for observations of objects like Comet Austin and the Sun.

articles.title: COMETS
articles.summary: This article highlights a technical report from the March 2, 1990 issue of SCIENCE journal, detailing "The Strange Periodic Comet Machholz." The report describes Comet Machholz 1988VIII (1986VI) as a unique object for studying cometary evolution due to its exceptionally close orbit to the Sun, tighter than any known planet or short-period comet.

articles.title: PLUTO
articles.summary: May offers a unique opportunity to observe Pluto, as it will be closer to Earth than it has been in 248 years. Stargazers are advised to consult finder charts in the May issues of Sky & Telescope or Astronomy magazines, or seek assistance from astronomy club officers.

articles.title: METEORS
articles.summary: The Eta Aquarid meteor shower, caused by Comet Halley, is scheduled to peak on May 4th, offering a rate of 20-40 meteors per hour. The article encourages observers to submit their results, even humorously suggesting creative viewing methods like a hot tub for this major annual event.

articles.title: DEEP SKY CHALLENGE
articles.summary: The article presents a "Deep Sky Challenge" to observe "Polarissima Borealis," a 13.6 magnitude galaxy in Ursa Minor. This galaxy is significant for being the closest to the North Celestial Pole, with coordinates given as 11:50.2 +89:07, and hints at requiring a large telescope.

articles.title: STAR PARTIES VS. SOLITUDE
articles.summary: The article contrasts the social benefits of star parties with the profound concentration achieved through solitary astronomical observing. While star parties are valuable for public outreach and trying different instruments, the author emphasizes that a more intimate, uninterrupted experience is crucial for appreciating subtle celestial details. The piece also highlights the challenges solitary observers face due to public misunderstanding and negative encounters, making it difficult to find peaceful, dark observing locations.

articles.title: GREAT RED SPOT
articles.summary: This article marks the close of the 1989-90 viewing season for Jupiter's Great Red Spot and the unexpected fading of the South Equatorial Belt, urging observers to make final observations before the planet's lower position in the sky causes poor seeing conditions. The author provides tips for optimal viewing and thanks readers for their reports and questions, indicating a temporary break from writing on this topic.

articles.title: COMET COMMENTS
articles.summary: This article provides updates on current comet visibility, highlighting Comet Austin as a new, naked-eye object expected to offer a good show despite early brightness being due to volatile burn-off. It also discusses the favorable placement of Periodic Comet Schwassmann-Wachmann 3, the ongoing visibility of Comet Skorichenko-George, and the recent discovery and subsequent dimming of Comet Cernis-Kiuchi-Nakamura. Observational tips for viewing these celestial visitors are included.

articles.title: METEOR NOTES
articles.summary: This article provides a guide to meteor activity in May, primarily focusing on the Eta Aquarid meteor shower, which peaks on May 4th and is best viewed in the hours before morning twilight. It also mentions the newly discovered Halleyid shower around May 8th and other minor May showers. Additionally, the author recounts a vivid observation of a 'April Fireball' in late March.

articles.title: ASTRO ADS
articles.summary: ASTRO ADS offers free advertising for non-commercial, astronomy-related products and services. Advertisers should submit their ads to Editor John P. Gleason by the 15th of each month for an approximate three-month run.

articles.title: BACK ISSUES OF DEEP SKY WANTED
articles.summary: Pat Donnelly is looking to borrow back issues of Deep Sky magazine. Individuals who can lend these magazines are encouraged to contact Pat at 408-778-2741.

articles.title: MEADE
articles.summary: This document functions as a classifieds section for used astronomical equipment, offering a diverse range of items for sale. Listings include various Meade and Celestron telescopes (e.g., LX3, C-90, C8), optical components like lenses and mirrors, and numerous accessories such as eyepieces, filters, and mounts. Additionally, it features free astronomy software, a request for a specific telescope part, and contact information for reporting fireballs.

articles.title: HUBBLE LAUNCH DELAYED
articles.summary: The launch of the Hubble Space Telescope was delayed from April 10 due to a faulty Auxiliary Power Unit (APU), requiring an eight-day process to recharge the telescope's batteries. This launch will place the shuttle into its highest-ever orbit for deployment. Following deployment, astronauts plan to utilize this high altitude to study large geological and oceanographic features on Earth.

articles.title: GIOTTO RETARGETED FOR COMET FLYBY
articles.summary: The European Space Agency's Giotto spacecraft, after its 1986 flyby of Comet Halley, has been retargeted for a second comet encounter with Comet Grigg-Skjellerup on July 10, 1992. The mission includes an Earth gravity assist on July 2, 1992, and despite some instrument damage from its Halley encounter, several key scientific instruments, including the high-resolution camera, remain operational.

articles.title: JUPITER'S RED SPOT
articles.summary: This document presents a schedule detailing the predicted times when Jupiter's Great Red Spot (GRS) will be on the meridian during various dates in May. The times are provided in Pacific Standard Time (PST), serving as a guide for observers interested in viewing this prominent planetary feature.

articles.title: CONSUMER SCIENTIFIC
articles.summary: Consumer Scientific is a retailer offering a wide array of science and nature products for both hobbyists and professionals. Their product range includes optics, books, science kits, labware, chemicals, maps, globes, and weather instruments. The ad provides contact information, including a phone number and a physical address in Mountain View, CA.

articles.title: MUSES-A IN LUNAR ORBIT
articles.summary: The Japanese Muses-A subsatellite successfully entered lunar orbit on March 19th, making Japan the third nation, after the U.S. and the Soviet Union, to send a spacecraft to the Moon. This achievement marks a significant milestone in space exploration.

articles.title: PEGASUS MAKES ORBITAL FLIGHT
articles.summary: The Pegasus air-launched booster successfully placed a payload into Low-Earth polar orbit on April 5th. This privately developed booster was deployed from a carrier airplane at 40,000 ft and 0.8 Mach, using a winged first stage for enhanced lift. Pegasus is designed to deliver approximately 900 lbs into low Earth orbit.

articles.title: NASA CONSIDERING RESCUE
articles.summary: An Intelsat 6 spacecraft was left in a useless orbit on March 14 after an incorrectly wired Titan 3 booster forced it to detach without its perigee motor. NASA is considering a shuttle mission in late 1990 or early 1991 to either retrieve the stranded spacecraft or attach a new perigee motor to rectify its orbit.

articles.title: SOVIET SPACE PROGRAM
articles.summary: The Soviet Mir space station successfully grew protein crystals for a U.S. company. The Buran shuttle will not be launched again due to a lack of critical systems and high modification costs, though a new unmanned orbiter is slated for 1991. Furthermore, an exhibit showcasing Soviet space technology, including models of Sputnik and Mir, is being prepared for display at the Bonton Museum of Science this summer.

articles.title: OFFICERS AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
articles.summary: This document lists the current officers and board of directors for an organization. It provides their names, titles (such as President, Vice President, Treasurer, Secretary, Editor, and Director), and respective contact phone numbers. This information outlines the key leadership positions and their contact details.

articles.title: EPHEMERIS CONTRIBUTORS
articles.summary: This document lists individuals credited as "Ephemeris Contributors," providing their names along with several associated phone numbers. It appears to serve as a directory or acknowledgment of those who contribute to the creation or maintenance of an ephemeris.

articles.title: COMET EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: This document provides an astronomical ephemeris detailing the positions and magnitudes of three comets: Comet Austin (1989c₁), Comet Skortchenko-George (1989s₁), and Periodic Comet Schwassmann-Wachmann 3 (1989d₁). For dates spanning late April to early June, it lists celestial coordinates (RA, DEC for both 1950 and 2000 epochs), elongation from the Sun, sky visibility (morning/evening), and apparent magnitude. This data is essential for astronomers and observers tracking these comets.

articles.title: THIS MONTH'S METEORS
articles.summary: This document provides a detailed list of meteor showers for a specific month, outlining key observational data. For each shower, it includes the start, maximum, and end dates, the estimated hourly rate, and the radiant's right ascension and declination, serving as a comprehensive guide for stargazers.

articles.title: DOUBLE, TRIPLE, AND MULTIPLE STARS
articles.summary: This article provides an observing guide for amateur astronomers, focusing on bright double, triple, and multiple star systems that are ideal targets during moonlit spring nights when dim galaxies are less visible. It highlights specific celestial objects such as Castor, Mizar, Xi Ursa Majoris, Gamma Leonis, and Cor Caroli, detailing their magnitudes, separations, and unique observing characteristics. The author encourages consistent observation of these fascinating multi-star systems, especially those with changing positions like Xi Ursa Majoris.

articles.title: FROM THE COSMIC MIND BOGGLING BOOK
articles.summary: This article from "The Cosmic Mind Boggling Book" details several astonishing facts about the Milky Way Galaxy, including its slow rotation rate over cosmic timescales and its rapid but still 'turtle-paced' velocity through the universe. It highlights the immense scale of the galaxy, the challenges of observing its full extent due to gas and dust, and the structure of its spiral arms, noting the Sun's location in the Orion arm and the roles of optical and radio astronomy in mapping it.

articles.title: The Tenth Annual Bay Area Astronomical Auction
articles.summary: The Tenth Annual Bay Area Astronomical Auction is approaching, offering participants an opportunity to sell astronomical or telescope-making related items for cash, with a 10% commission supporting public astronomy education. The event includes pre-registration for auction items, a Swap Meet for lower-value or specialized items, and a Silent Bid option for big-ticket items like complete telescopes. Sellers must pre-register items by mail with a SASE to receive item numbers.

articles.title: DIRECTIONS to the Red Cross building
articles.summary: This document provides detailed directions to the Red Cross building at 14011 Los Gatos-Saratoga Rd. for the 1990 SJAA (San Jose Astronomical Association) auction and swap meet. The event includes a swap meet from 2 to 5 pm, an auction starting at 6 pm, and requests a $1 donation for registration to buy or sell. Refreshments will be available, and car-pooling is encouraged.

articles.title: SAN JOSE ASTRONOMICAL ASSOCIATION MEMBERSHIP APPLICATION
articles.summary: This document is a membership application for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA), detailing various membership types including 'Membership Only,' 'Membership/S&T,' and 'Junior (Under 18),' along with their respective costs. It provides instructions for submitting the form and payment, and lists contact information for the Treasurer. Additionally, it contains publication details for the 'SJAA EPHEMERIS,' a monthly newsletter, including submission guidelines for articles.
